An AI can now redraw what you're looking at, straight from your brain scan.
It's called Brain-IT, from Michal Irani's lab at the Weizmann Institute.
Volunteers lay in an fMRI scanner and viewed thousands of photos, while it logged blood flow in tiny cubes of brain called voxels.
The scanner never sees a picture. It only sees where oxygen use rises and falls.
So the AI learns the pattern. One branch guesses what is in the scene. Another guesses its layout and colors.
Then a diffusion model, the noise-removal trick behind AI art, paints the image from those two clues.
It needs about an hour of scanning from a new person, where older methods trained on forty.
It still slips: a dog in a bathtub came out as a goat. And it decodes pictures people saw, not dreams.
But as brain decoding improves, who gets to read a brain becomes a real question.
